summary: Specifies the SIP P-Private-Network-Indication P-header used by 3GPP to mark a message as part of a private network's traffic and identify that network, so nodes can apply different rules.

eli5.summary: A letter can have a sticker saying it belongs to a particular company's private mail. Then the post office handles it by that company's rules.

questions: how does sip mark enterprise traffic
when is break-in used in networks
what is a trust domain in sip
subtitle: Marking SIP messages for handling within private telecommunications networks.

tldr.problem: In 3GPP networks, operators need to distinguish private enterprise network traffic from public network traffic and apply different rules to each.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7316 defines a SIP header field called P-Private-Network-Indication that carries a domain name to mark a message as belonging to a specific private network.
tldr.outcome: Network nodes that recognize this header can apply enterprise-specific processing rules, handle break-in and break-out scenarios, and enable hosted services for business communication.

today: RFC 7316 is an Informational RFC published in July 2014 and has not been obsoleted. It is used in 3GPP IMS deployments and ETSI TISPAN networks for marking enterprise call traffic.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 7316 specifies the P-Private-Network-Indication header field for use in the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP), a signaling protocol used in telecommunications. This header was defined by 3GPP, a standard organization that develops specifications for cellular networks.

The header identifies that a SIP message belongs to the traffic of a specific private network and enables network nodes to apply different processing rules to that traffic compared to public network traffic. The private network is identified by a domain name value in the header.
sections.eli5: SIP is used by phone systems to set up calls. This header lets a message say 'I belong to this company' so routers know to apply that company's special rules.

sections.title: Definitions and Scope
sections.content:
The RFC defines key terms for understanding private networks in SIP environments. Public network traffic is sent to or received from a public telecommunication network using standard rules for ordinary subscribers. Private network traffic is handled according to rules specific to an enterprise or group of related enterprises.

Two important operations are break-in, where a node converts incoming public network traffic to private network traffic by adding the header, and break-out, where a node removes the header to convert private network traffic to public traffic before forwarding it outside the trust domain.

The header is restricted to use within a trust domain, a set of network nodes that trust each other. The specification applies specifically to 3GPP IP Multimedia Subsystem (IMS) and similar controlled networks.
sections.eli5: Think of it like postage: some mail is labeled 'company internal' and some is public. When mail leaves the building, the company label is removed.

sections.title: Header Format and Operation
sections.content:
The P-Private-Network-Indication header contains a hostname value that serves as the private network identifier. For example: P-Private-Network-Indication: example.com.

Using a domain name as the identifier offers two advantages: it becomes a globally unique identifier that can be associated with enterprises, and it reuses domain names already owned by organizations without requiring a separate registry. When an enterprise needs multiple identifiers, it can freely add subdomains.

The header field follows RFC 3261 (SIP) syntax rules and can be extended with optional parameters if needed. Proxies may insert the header into initial requests for dialogs or standalone transactions based on authentication, configuration, or local policy.
sections.eli5: The header is just a company's domain name, like 'acme.com'. It is simple and lets companies use domain names they already own.

sections.title: Proxy Behavior and Trust
sections.content:
Proxies (SIP intermediaries) have specific responsibilities when handling this header. A proxy that determines traffic should be private must insert the header. A proxy that receives the header from an untrusted node must remove it; the header MUST NOT be used from untrusted sources because spoofing could allow attackers to inject false network traffic claims.

When forwarding a message to untrusted proxies or entities outside the trust domain, the receiving proxy MUST remove the header. The specification requires proxies to verify that received domain names match provisioned values, removing the header if they do not match.

This trust-domain enforcement is critical for security: if the indication leaked outside the trust domain, it could reveal sensitive information about an organization's internal call routing, potentially enabling attacks or compromising privacy.
sections.eli5: The header only works between trusted routers. If a message leaves the company network, the label is removed. Untrusted computers cannot use this label or they would fake who they are.

sections.title: Security and Deployment Implications
sections.content:
The specification emphasizes that the header must only be used between mutually trusted network elements. Protection can be achieved through protocols like SIP/TLS (Transport Layer Security) or IP Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP), or through physical network isolation.

A critical security risk exists if the indication propagates outside its trust domain: it may reveal the caller's organization identity and indicate that different rules apply to the call. To prevent breaches, proxies must not insert the header when forwarding to nodes outside the trust domain and must remove it before forwarding to untrusted nodes.

The RFC notes that the P-Private-Network-Indication header is not intended for the general Internet environment due to lack of spoofing prevention mechanisms. Without proper trust domain enforcement, an attacker could inject false network indications and compromise private network processing.
sections.eli5: This only works in closed company networks, not the open internet. If hackers could fake this label, they could trick routers into applying the wrong rules to their calls.
